      • Sort out the ten most spoken languages by location.
      • Sort out the ten most populated countries.

    4.3 Python Error Types

    Python Error Types

    When we write code it is common that we make a typo or some other common error. If our code fails to run, the Python interpreter will display a message, containing feedback with information on where the problem occurs and the type of an error. It will also sometimes gives us suggestions on a possible fix. Understanding different types of errors in programming languages will help us to debug our code quickly and also it makes us better at what we do.

    Let us see the most common error types one by one. First let us open our Python interactive shell. Go to your computer terminal (or the Python Console in PyCharm) and type ‘python’. The python interactive shell will be opened.

    SyntaxError

    Example 1: SyntaxError

    PYTHON 

    >>> print 'hello world'
  File "<stdin>", line 1
    print 'hello world'
    ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
SyntaxError: Missing parentheses in call to 'print'. Did you mean print(...)?
>>>

    As you can see we made a syntax error because we forgot to enclose the string with parenthesis and Python already suggests the solution. Let us fix it.

    PYTHON 

    >>> print 'hello world'
  File "<stdin>", line 1
    print 'hello world'
    ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
SyntaxError: Missing parentheses in call to 'print'. Did you mean print(...)?
>>> print('hello world')
hello world
>>>

    The error was a SyntaxError. After the fix our code was executed without a hitch. Let see more error types.

    NameError

    Example 1: NameError

    PYTHON 

    >>> print(age)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
NameError: name 'age' is not defined
>>>

    As you can see from the message above, name age is not defined. Yes, it is true that we did not define an age variable but we were trying to print it out as if we had had declared it. Now, lets fix this by declaring it and assigning with a value.

    PYTHON 

    >>> print(age)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
NameError: name 'age' is not defined
>>> age = 25
>>> print(age)
25
>>>

    The type of error was a NameError. We debugged the error by defining the variable name.

    IndexError

    Example 1: IndexError

    PYTHON 

    >>> numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
>>> numbers[5]
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
IndexError: list index out of range
>>>

    In the example above, Python raised an IndexError, because the list has only indexes from 0 to 4 , so it was out of range.

    ModuleNotFoundError

    Example 1: ModuleNotFoundError

    PYTHON 

    >>> import maths
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'maths'
>>>

    In the example above, I added an extra s to math deliberately and ModuleNotFoundError was raised. Lets fix it by removing the extra s from math.

    PYTHON 

    >>> import maths
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'maths'
>>> import math
>>>

    We fixed it, so let’s use some of the functions from the math module.

    AttributeError

    Example 1: AttributeError

    PYTHON 

    >>> import maths
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'maths'
>>> import math
>>> math.PI
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
AttributeError: module 'math' has no attribute 'PI'. Did you mean: 'pi'?
>>>

    As you can see, I made a mistake again! Instead of pi, I tried to call a PI constant from the math module. It raised an attribute error, it means, that the attribute does not exist in the module. Lets fix it by changing from PI to pi.

    PYTHON 

    >>> import maths
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'maths'
>>> import math
>>> math.PI
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
AttributeError: module 'math' has no attribute 'PI'. Did you mean: 'pi'?
>>> math.pi
3.141592653589793
>>>

    Now, when we call pi from the math module we got the result.

    KeyError

    Example 1: KeyError

    PYTHON 

    >>> users = {'name':'Sam', 'age':25, 'country':'Australia'}
>>> users['name']
'Sam'
>>> users['county']
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
KeyError: 'county'
>>>

    As you can see, there was a typo in the key used to get the dictionary value. so, this is a key error and the fix is quite straight forward. Let’s do this!

    PYTHON 

    >>> user = {'name':'Sam', 'age':25, 'country':'Australia'}
>>> user['name']
'Sam'
>>> user['county']
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
KeyError: 'county'
>>> user['country']
'Australia'
>>>

    We debugged the error, our code ran and we got the value.

    TypeError

    Example 1: TypeError

    PYTHON 

    >>> 4 + '3'
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'int' and 'str'
>>>

    In the example above, a TypeError is raised because we cannot add a number to a string. First solution would be to convert the string to int or float. Another solution would be converting the number to a string (the result then would be ‘43’). Let us follow the first fix.

    PYTHON 

    >>> 4 + '3'
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'int' and 'str'
>>> 4 + int('3')
7
>>> 4 + float('3')
7.0
>>>

    Error removed and we got the result we expected.

    ImportError

    Example 1: ImportError

    PYTHON 

    >>> from math import power
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
ImportError: cannot import name 'power' from 'math' (unknown location)
>>>

    There is no function called power in the math module, it goes with a different name: pow. Let’s correct it:

    PYTHON 

    >>> from math import power
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
ImportError: cannot import name 'power' from 'math' (unknown location)
>>> from math import pow
>>> pow(2,3)
8.0
>>>

    ValueError

    PYTHON 

    >>> int('12a')
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '12a'
>>>

    In this case we cannot change the given string to a number, because of the ‘a’ letter in it.

    ZeroDivisionError

    PYTHON 

    >>> 1/0
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
ZeroDivisionError: division by zero
>>>

    We cannot divide a number by zero.

    We have covered some of the python error types, if you want to check more about it check the python documentation about python error types. If you are good at reading the error types, then you will be able to fix your bugs fast and you will also become a better programmer.

    Challenge

    Exercises

    1. Open your Python interactive shell and try all the examples covered in this section.

    4.4 Exception Handling

    Exception Handling

    Python uses try and except to handle errors gracefully. A graceful exit (or graceful handling) of errors is a simple programming idiom - a program detects a serious error condition and “exits gracefully”, in a controlled manner as a result. Often the program prints a descriptive error message to a terminal or log as part of the graceful exit, this makes our application more robust. The cause of an exception is often external to the program itself. An example of exceptions could be an incorrect input, wrong file name, unable to find a file, a malfunctioning IO device. Graceful handling of errors prevents our applications from crashing.

    We have covered the different Python error types in the previous section. If we use try and except in our program, then it will not raise errors in those blocks.

    PYTHON 

    try:
    ...  # Run this code
except ValueError:  # the exception name is optional
    ...  # Run this code when there is an exception
else:
    ...  # No exception? Run this code
finally:
    ...  # Always run this code

    PYTHON 

    # syntax
try:
    code in this block runs if things go well
except:
    code in this block runs if things go wrong

    Example:

    PYTHON 

    try:
    print(10 + '5')
except:
    print('Something went wrong')
# Something went wrong

    In the example above the second operand is a string. We could change it to float or int to add it with the number to make it work. But without any changes, the second block, except, will be executed.

    Example:

    PYTHON 

    try:
    name = input('Enter your name:')
    year_born = input('Year you were born:')
    age = 2026 - year_born
    print(f'You are {name}. And your age is {age}.')
except:
    print('Something went wrong')

    OUTPUT 

    Enter your name:Jack
Year you were born:2001
Something went wrong

    In the above example, the exception block will run and we do not know exactly the problem. To analyze the problem, we can use the different error types with except.

    In the following example, it will handle the error and will also tell us the kind of error raised.

    PYTHON 

    try:
    name = input('Enter your name:')
    year_born = input('Year you were born:')
    age = 2026 - year_born
    print(f'You are {name}. And your age is {age}.')
except TypeError:
    print('Type error occurred')
except ValueError:
    print('Value error occurred')
except ZeroDivisionError:
    print('Zero division error occurred')

    OUTPUT 

    Enter your name:Jack
Year you were born:2001
Type error occurred

    In the code above the output is going to be TypeError. Now, let’s add an additional block:

    PYTHON 

    try:
    name = input('Enter your name:')
    year_born = input('Year you were born:')
    age = 2026 - int(year_born)
    print(f'You are {name}. And your age is {age}.')
except TypeError:
    print('Type error occurred')
except ValueError:
    print('Value error occurred')
except ZeroDivisionError:
    print('Zero division error occurred')
else:
    print('I usually run with the try block')
finally:
    print('I always run.')

    OUTPUT 

    Enter your name:Jack
Year you were born:2001
You are Jack. And your age is 25.
I usually run with the try block
I always run.

    We can also shorten the above code as follows:

    PYTHON 

    try:
    name = input('Enter your name:')
    year_born = input('Year you were born:')
    age = 2026 - int(year_born)
    print(f'You are {name}. And your age is {age}.')
except Exception as e:
    print(e)

    Packing and Unpacking Arguments in Python

    We use two operators:

    • * for tuples
    • ** for dictionaries

    Let us take as an example below. It takes only arguments but we have list. We can unpack the list and changes to argument.

    Unpacking

    Unpacking Lists

    PYTHON 

    def sum_of_five_nums(a, b, c, d, e):
    return a + b + c + d + e

lst = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
# print(sum_of_five_nums(lst))  # this would give: TypeError: sum_of_five_nums() missing 4 required positional arguments: 'b', 'c', 'd', and 'e'

    If we ran this code, it would raise an error, because this function takes numbers (not a list) as arguments. Let us unpack/destructure the list.

    PYTHON 

    def sum_of_five_nums(a, b, c, d, e):
    return a + b + c + d + e

lst = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
print(sum_of_five_nums(*lst))  # 15

    We can also use unpacking in the range built-in function that expects a start and an end.

    PYTHON 

    numbers = range(2, 7)  # normal call with separate arguments
print(list(numbers)) # [2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
args = [2, 7]
numbers = range(*args)  # call with arguments unpacked from a list
print(list(numbers))  # [2, 3, 4, 5, 6]

    A list or a tuple can also be unpacked like this:

    PYTHON 

    countries = ['Australia', 'New Zealand', 'Fiji', 'Samoa', 'Tonga']
aus, nz, fiji, *rest = countries
print(aus, nz, fiji, rest)   # Australia New Zealand Fiji ['Samoa', 'Tonga']
numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]
one, *middle, last = numbers
print(one, middle, last)      # 1 [2, 3, 4, 5, 6] 7
    Unpacking Dictionaries

    PYTHON 

    def unpacking_person_info(name, country, city, age):
    return f'{name} lives in {city}, {country}. He is {age} years old.'
dct = {'name':'Jack', 'country':'Australia', 'city':'Perth', 'age':25}
print(unpacking_person_info(**dct)) # Jack lives in Perth, Australia. He is 25 years old.

    Packing

    Sometimes we never know how many arguments need to be passed to a python function. We can use the packing method to allow our function to take unlimited number or arbitrary number of arguments.

    Packing Lists

    PYTHON 

    def sum_all(*args):
    s = 0
    for i in args:
        s += i
    return s
print(sum_all(1, 2, 3))             # 6
print(sum_all(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7)) # 28
    Packing Dictionaries

    PYTHON 

    def packing_person_info(**kwargs):
    # check the type of kwargs and it is a dict type
    # print(type(kwargs))
    # Printing dictionary items
    for key in kwargs:
        print(f"{key} = {kwargs[key]}")
    return kwargs

print(packing_person_info(name="Jack",
      country="Australia", city="Perth", age=25))

    OUTPUT 

    name = Jack
country = Australia
city = Perth
age = 25
{'name': 'Jack', 'country': 'Australia', 'city': 'Perth', 'age': 25}

    Spreading in Python

    Like in JavaScript, spreading is possible in Python. Let us check it in an example below:

    PYTHON 

    lst_one = [1, 2, 3]
lst_two = [4, 5, 6, 7]
lst = [0, *lst_one, *lst_two]
print(lst)          # [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]
country_lst_one = ['Australia', 'New Zealand']
country_lst_two = ['Fiji', 'Samoa', 'Tonga']
oceania_countries = [*country_lst_one, *country_lst_two]
print(oceania_countries)  # ['Australia', 'New Zealand', 'Fiji', 'Samoa', 'Tonga']

    Enumerate

    If we are interested in an index of a list, we use enumerate built-in function to get the index of each item in the list.

    PYTHON 

    for index, item in enumerate([20, 30, 40]):
    print(index, item)
# 0 20
# 1 30
# 2 40

    PYTHON 

    countries = ['Australia', 'New Zealand', 'Fiji', 'Samoa', 'Tonga']
for index, i in enumerate(countries):
    if i == 'Fiji':
        print(f'The country {i} has been found at index {index}')

    OUTPUT 

    The country Fiji has been found at index 2

    Zip

    Sometimes we would like to combine lists when looping through them. See the example below:

    PYTHON 

    fruits = ['banana', 'orange', 'mango', 'lemon', 'lime']                    
vegetables = ['Tomato', 'Potato', 'Cabbage','Onion', 'Carrot']
fruits_and_veges = []
for f, v in zip(fruits, vegetables):
    fruits_and_veges.append({'fruit':f, 'veg':v})

print(fruits_and_veges)

    OUTPUT 

    [{'fruit': 'banana', 'veg': 'Tomato'}, {'fruit': 'orange', 'veg': 'Potato'}, {'fruit': 'mango', 'veg': 'Cabbage'}, {'fruit': 'lemon', 'veg': 'Onion'}, {'fruit': 'lime', 'veg': 'Carrot'}]
    Challenge

    Exercises

    1. names = [‘Australia’, ‘New Zealand’, ‘Fiji’, ‘Samoa’, ‘Tonga’, ‘Japan’, ‘China’]. Unpack the first five countries and store them in a variable oceania_countries, store Japan and China in jp and cn respectively.

    Concepts Bridge: Functional and Logic Programming

    Time: 30 minutes (2 min functional ideas, 8 min video, 4 min SWISH, 1 min Python version, 15 min activity)

    Why this matters

    Python can be used in a functional way, even though it is also object-oriented. This supports LO 2 (apply object-oriented, imperative, functional and logic programming techniques). Today you meet two paradigms (styles of programming): functional and logic.

    Functional ideas (2 min)

    A side effect is anything a function does besides returning a value, such as printing or changing a list outside the function. A pure function has no side effects: the same input always gives the same answer.

    PYTHON 

    def add_gst_pure(price):
    return round(price * 1.1, 2)      # pure: only uses its input


def add_gst_impure(price, log):
    total = round(price * 1.1, 2)
    log.append(total)                 # side effect: changes a list outside
    return total


history = []
print(add_gst_pure(100))              # 110.0
print(add_gst_impure(100, history))   # 110.0
print(add_gst_impure(50, history))    # 55.0
print(history)                        # [110.0, 55.0] (the outside list changed)

    Pure functions are easy to test, because you only check input and output.

    Recursion means a function calls itself on a smaller problem. It needs a base case, the simple answer that stops the calls.

    PYTHON 

    def add_up(items):
    if not items:                          # base case: empty list
        return 0
    return items[0] + add_up(items[1:])    # smaller problem


print(add_up([4, 5, 6]))  # 15

    There is no changing variable. This is why functional languages like recursion.

    Logic programming (LO 2)

    In logic programming you do not write steps. You state facts (things that are true) and rules (how new facts follow from old ones). Then you ask queries (questions) and the system searches for answers. Prolog is the best-known logic language.

    Video (8 min)

    [Programming Epitome] Prolog Programming Basics: Facts, Rules and Queries (7:57) https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4F2FLNQ6yms

    Watch for: how a fact, a rule and a query look, and how Prolog finds the answers by itself.

    Run it: a family tree in Prolog (4 min)

    1. Open SWISH: https://swish.swi-prolog.org/ (free, runs in your browser, no account needed to run queries). If it shows a welcome page, choose to create a new Prolog program.
    2. Paste this program into the editor (the main text area).

    PROLOG 

    parent(tom, bob).
parent(tom, liz).
parent(bob, ann).
parent(bob, pat).

grandparent(X, Z) :- parent(X, Y), parent(Y, Z).

ancestor(X, Z) :- parent(X, Z).
ancestor(X, Z) :- parent(X, Y), ancestor(Y, Z).

    :- means “is true if”. Names starting with a capital letter (X, Y, Z) are variables. Every line ends with a full stop.

    1. In the query box at the bottom right, type grandparent(tom, Who). and click Run!. You should see Who = ann, then use Next to see Who = pat.
    2. Now run ancestor(tom, Who). and click Next to see every answer. Notice you did not write any search steps. Prolog found the answers itself.

    The same idea in Python (1 min)

    Facts are a set of tuples. Rules are functions. Queries are function calls. Run this with python -I or in PyCharm.

    PYTHON 

    # Facts: (parent, child)
parent_facts = {
    ("tom", "bob"),
    ("tom", "liz"),
    ("bob", "ann"),
    ("bob", "pat"),
}


# Rules
def is_parent(x, y):
    return (x, y) in parent_facts


def children(x):
    return sorted([c for (p, c) in parent_facts if p == x])


def is_sibling(a, b):
    if a == b:
        return False
    for (p, child) in parent_facts:
        if child == a and is_parent(p, b):
            return True
    return False


# Queries
print(is_parent("tom", "bob"))    # True
print(children("tom"))            # ['bob', 'liz']
print(is_sibling("ann", "pat"))   # True
print(is_sibling("ann", "liz"))   # False

    In Prolog you write the rule once and the system does the searching. In Python you write the search yourself with a for loop. Python is not a logic language, but you can copy the idea.

    Challenge

    Activity (15 min)

    Use the Python code above as your starting point.

    1. Add the fact that liz is the parent of joe.
    2. Write a rule is_grandparent(x, z) that returns True or False. Loop over parent_facts, use is_parent, and keep it pure (no printing, no changing parent_facts).
    3. Write a recursive rule is_ancestor(x, z). An ancestor is a parent, or a parent of an ancestor. Hint: return True straight away if x is a parent of z. Otherwise use a for loop over the facts, and for each child y of x, ask is_ancestor(y, z). If nothing works, return False.
    4. Test: is tom an ancestor of ann? Of joe? Is ann an ancestor of tom?
    5. In one or two sentences: which parts of your answer are functional, and which are logic-style?

    PYTHON 

    parent_facts = {
    ("tom", "bob"),
    ("tom", "liz"),
    ("bob", "ann"),
    ("bob", "pat"),
    ("liz", "joe"),   # new fact
}


def is_parent(x, y):
    return (x, y) in parent_facts


def is_grandparent(x, z):
    for (p, y) in parent_facts:
        if p == x and is_parent(y, z):
            return True
    return False


def is_ancestor(x, z):
    if is_parent(x, z):                      # base case
        return True
    for (p, y) in parent_facts:              # recursive case
        if p == x and is_ancestor(y, z):
            return True
    return False


print(is_grandparent("tom", "joe"))  # True
print(is_ancestor("tom", "ann"))     # True
print(is_ancestor("tom", "joe"))     # True
print(is_ancestor("ann", "tom"))     # False

    Note: the rules are pure functions that only read the facts, and is_ancestor uses recursion, so they are functional. The facts-rules-queries layout is logic-style, but Python needs us to write the search ourselves, whereas Prolog does it for us.

    Further reading

    • Programming Epitome (n.d.) Prolog Programming Basics: Facts, Rules and Queries [Video]. YouTube. Available at: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4F2FLNQ6yms (Accessed: 2 November 2026).
    • Driscoll, M. (2017) Python 101. Available at: https://web.archive.org/web/20260309033724/https://python101.pythonlibrary.org/ (Accessed: 2 November 2026).

    Practice task: Functional Grade Calculator

    Callout

    Files for this task

    Download these files into a folder for this task and open the folder in PyCharm.

    • starter.py
    • solution.py
    • test_solution.py

    Time: about 2 hours. This is a practice task. It is not marked.

    Goal

    Take a short grade calculator written with loops and rewrite it in a functional style. Then make it safe against bad input with try / except.

    You do not need your Week 3 files. The Week 3 version is already inside starter.py (Part A).

    Files

    File What it is
    starter.py Part A: the loop version (given). Part B: your functions to fill in.
    test_solution.py Tests for the functions.
    solution.py A model answer. Try the task yourself before you look.

    Steps

    1. Read Part A in starter.py. To try it, scroll to the last line of the file and temporarily change main() to main_loop(). Run the file, then type abc when it asks for a mark. It crashes. That is the problem we will fix. Change the last line back to main() before you carry on.
      • Near the bottom you will see if __name__ == "__main__":. Leave those two lines as they are. They mean “run this when the file is run directly”, and Week 6 explains how they work.
    2. In Part B, write parse_mark(text). Use try / except ValueError. Return None for text that is not a number, or a number outside 0 to 100. Otherwise return the mark as a float.
    3. Write valid_marks(texts) with a list comprehension. Use map(parse_mark, texts) and drop the None values.
    4. Write average(marks). Use try / except ZeroDivisionError so an empty list gives 0.0.
    5. Write grade(mark). Copy the if/elif logic from Part A.
    6. Write letter_grades(marks) with map().
    7. Write passing_marks(marks) with filter() and a lambda.
    8. Write grade_counts(marks) with a dictionary comprehension over GRADE_ORDER.
    9. Write main(). Ask for marks until an empty line. Tell the user when a mark is not valid and carry on. Print the results.
    10. Write your 5-sentence note (see below).

    Example run

    OUTPUT 

    Enter marks from 0 to 100. Press Enter on an empty line to finish.
Mark: 90
Mark: abc
  Not a valid mark, ignoring it.
Mark: 55
Mark: 120
  Not a valid mark, ignoring it.
Mark:
Average: 72.5
Grades: ['HD', 'P']
Passing marks: [90.0, 55.0]
Grade counts: {'HD': 1, 'D': 0, 'C': 0, 'P': 1, 'F': 0}

    Your wording can differ.

    Hints

    • float("abc") raises a ValueError. That is the error you catch.
    • [m for m in map(f, items) if m is not None] keeps only the answers that are not None.
    • list(map(grade, marks)) and list(filter(lambda m: m >= 50, marks)) need list(...) to give you a list.
    • grades.count("HD") counts how many times "HD" appears in a list.
    • A dictionary comprehension builds a dictionary in one line, like a list comprehension but with key: value. For example, {g: grades.count(g) for g in GRADE_ORDER} makes a dictionary with one entry per grade in GRADE_ORDER, where each value is how often that grade appears in grades. (Here grades is the list of letter grades you get from letter_grades(marks).)
    • Keep input() and print() inside main() only. Functions that only take input and return output are pure and easy to test.

    Your 5-sentence note

    Write five sentences, in a file or a comment at the bottom of your code, comparing the loop version (Part A) with your functional version (Part B). You could cover:

    1. Which version is shorter?
    2. Which is easier to read, and for whom?
    3. Which is easier to test, and why?
    4. What did try / except change for the user?
    5. Which style would you choose for this problem, and why?

    Check your work

    Key Points
    • Each week has four blocks: Watch, Read & practise, Concepts Bridge and Build.
    • [expression for item in iterable if condition] builds a new list.
    • A lambda is a small function written in one expression.
    • Functions are values: you can pass them around.
    • map() changes every item, filter() keeps some items, reduce() combines items into one value.
    • The last line of a traceback names the error type.
    • Read error messages carefully: Python often suggests the fix.
    • try runs risky code; except handles the error.
    • Catch the specific error you expect, not every error.
      • unpacks lists and ** unpacks dictionaries.
    • A pure function has no side effects.
    • Recursion solves a problem by calling the function on a smaller problem.
    • Logic programming states facts and rules, then asks questions.
    • The same problem can be solved in more than one style.

    5.1 Classes and Objects

    Classes and Objects

    Python is an object oriented programming language. Everything in Python is an object, with its properties and methods. A number, string, list, dictionary, tuple, set etc. used in a program is an object of a corresponding built-in class. We create class to create an object. A class is like an object constructor, or a “blueprint” for creating objects. We instantiate a class to create an object. The class defines attributes and the behavior of the object, while the object, on the other hand, represents the class.

    We have been working with classes and objects right from the beginning of this challenge unknowingly. Every element in a Python program is an object of a class. Let us check if everything in python is a class:

    PYTHON 

    student@adci:~$ python
Python 3.9.6 (default, Jun 28 2021, 15:26:21)
[Clang 11.0.0 (clang-1100.0.33.8)] on darwin
Type "help", "copyright", "credits" or "license" for more information.
>>> num = 10
>>> type(num)
<class 'int'>
>>> string = 'string'
>>> type(string)
<class 'str'>
>>> boolean = True
>>> type(boolean)
<class 'bool'>
>>> lst = []
>>> type(lst)
<class 'list'>
>>> tpl = ()
>>> type(tpl)
<class 'tuple'>
>>> set1 = set()
>>> type(set1)
<class 'set'>
>>> dct = {}
>>> type(dct)
<class 'dict'>

    Creating a Class

    To create a class we need the key word class followed by the name and colon. Class name should be CamelCase.

    PYTHON 

    # syntax
class ClassName:
    code goes here

    Example:

    PYTHON 

    class Person:
    pass

print(Person)

    OUTPUT 

    <class '__main__.Person'>

    Creating an Object

    We can create an object by calling the class.

    PYTHON 

    p = Person()
print(p)

    OUTPUT 

    <__main__.Person object at 0x10804e510>

    The number at the end is the object’s address in memory, so yours will be different.

    Class Constructor

    In the examples above, we have created an object from the Person class. However, a class without a constructor is not really useful in real applications. Let us use constructor function to make our class more useful. Like the constructor function in Java or JavaScript, Python has also a built-in init() constructor function. The init constructor function has self parameter which is a reference to the current instance of the class

    Examples:

    PYTHON 

    class Person:
    def __init__(self, name):
        # self allows to attach parameter to the class
        self.name = name

p = Person('Jack')
print(p.name)
print(p)

    OUTPUT 

    Jack
<__main__.Person object at 0x2abf46907e80>

    Let us add more parameters to the constructor function.

    PYTHON 

    class Person:
    def __init__(self, firstname, lastname, age, country, city):
        self.firstname = firstname
        self.lastname = lastname
        self.age = age
        self.country = country
        self.city = city

p = Person('Jack', 'Wilson', 25, 'Australia', 'Perth')
print(p.firstname)
print(p.lastname)
print(p.age)
print(p.country)
print(p.city)

    OUTPUT 

    Jack
Wilson
25
Australia
Perth

    Object Methods

    Objects can have methods. The methods are functions which belong to the object.

    Example:

    PYTHON 

    class Person:
    def __init__(self, firstname, lastname, age, country, city):
        self.firstname = firstname
        self.lastname = lastname
        self.age = age
        self.country = country
        self.city = city

    def person_info(self):
        return f'{self.firstname} {self.lastname} is {self.age} years old. He lives in {self.city}, {self.country}.'

p = Person('Jack', 'Wilson', 25, 'Australia', 'Perth')
print(p.person_info())

    OUTPUT 

    Jack Wilson is 25 years old. He lives in Perth, Australia.

    Object Default Methods

    Sometimes, you may want to have default values for your object methods. If we give default values for the parameters in the constructor, we can avoid errors when we call or instantiate our class without parameters. Let’s see how it looks:

    Example:

    PYTHON 

    class Person:
    def __init__(self, firstname='Jack', lastname='Wilson', age=25, country='Australia', city='Perth'):
        self.firstname = firstname
        self.lastname = lastname
        self.age = age
        self.country = country
        self.city = city

    def person_info(self):
        return f'{self.firstname} {self.lastname} is {self.age} years old. He lives in {self.city}, {self.country}.'

p1 = Person()
print(p1.person_info())
p2 = Person('Noah', 'Brown', 30, 'New Zealand', 'Auckland')
print(p2.person_info())

    OUTPUT 

    Jack Wilson is 25 years old. He lives in Perth, Australia.
Noah Brown is 30 years old. He lives in Auckland, New Zealand.

    Method to Modify Class Default Values

    In the example below, the person class, all the constructor parameters have default values. In addition to that, we have skills parameter, which we can access using a method. Let us create add_skill method to add skills to the skills list.

    PYTHON 

    class Person:
    def __init__(self, firstname='Jack', lastname='Wilson', age=25, country='Australia', city='Perth'):
        self.firstname = firstname
        self.lastname = lastname
        self.age = age
        self.country = country
        self.city = city
        self.skills = []

    def person_info(self):
        return f'{self.firstname} {self.lastname} is {self.age} years old. He lives in {self.city}, {self.country}.'

    def add_skill(self, skill):
        self.skills.append(skill)

p1 = Person()
print(p1.person_info())
p1.add_skill('Python')
p1.add_skill('Excel')
p1.add_skill('SQL')
p2 = Person('Noah', 'Brown', 30, 'New Zealand', 'Auckland')
print(p2.person_info())
print(p1.skills)
print(p2.skills)

    OUTPUT 

    Jack Wilson is 25 years old. He lives in Perth, Australia.
Noah Brown is 30 years old. He lives in Auckland, New Zealand.
['Python', 'Excel', 'SQL']
[]

    Inheritance

    Using inheritance we can reuse parent class code. Inheritance allows us to define a class that inherits all the methods and properties from parent class. The parent class or super or base class is the class which gives all the methods and properties. Child class is the class that inherits from another or parent class. Let us create a student class by inheriting from person class.

    PYTHON 

    class Student(Person):
    pass


s1 = Student('Liam', 'Taylor', 20, 'Australia', 'Perth')
s2 = Student('Olivia', 'Thompson', 19, 'Australia', 'Fremantle')
print(s1.person_info())
s1.add_skill('Python')
s1.add_skill('SQL')
s1.add_skill('Excel')
print(s1.skills)

print(s2.person_info())
s2.add_skill('Organising')
s2.add_skill('Marketing')
s2.add_skill('Digital Marketing')
print(s2.skills)

    OUTPUT 

    Liam Taylor is 20 years old. He lives in Perth, Australia.
['Python', 'SQL', 'Excel']
Olivia Thompson is 19 years old. He lives in Fremantle, Australia.
['Organising', 'Marketing', 'Digital Marketing']

    Notice that the output says “He” for Olivia too, because person_info() always uses “He”. We fix this below by overriding the method.

    We did not call the init() constructor in the child class. If we didn’t call it then we can still access all the properties from the parent. But if we do call the constructor we can access the parent properties by calling super. We can add a new method to the child or we can override the parent class methods by creating the same method name in the child class. When we add the init() function, the child class will no longer inherit the parent’s init() function.

    Overriding parent method

    PYTHON 

    class Student(Person):
    def __init__(self, firstname='Jack', lastname='Wilson', age=25, country='Australia', city='Perth', gender='male'):
        self.gender = gender
        super().__init__(firstname, lastname, age, country, city)

    def person_info(self):
        pronoun = 'He' if self.gender == 'male' else 'She'
        return f'{self.firstname} {self.lastname} is {self.age} years old. {pronoun} lives in {self.city}, {self.country}.'

s1 = Student('Liam', 'Taylor', 20, 'Australia', 'Perth', 'male')
s2 = Student('Olivia', 'Thompson', 19, 'Australia', 'Fremantle', 'female')
print(s1.person_info())
s1.add_skill('Python')
s1.add_skill('SQL')
s1.add_skill('Excel')
print(s1.skills)

print(s2.person_info())
s2.add_skill('Organising')
s2.add_skill('Marketing')
s2.add_skill('Digital Marketing')
print(s2.skills)

    OUTPUT 

    Liam Taylor is 20 years old. He lives in Perth, Australia.
['Python', 'SQL', 'Excel']
Olivia Thompson is 19 years old. She lives in Fremantle, Australia.
['Organising', 'Marketing', 'Digital Marketing']

    We can use super() built-in function or the parent name Person to automatically inherit the methods and properties from its parent. In the example above we override the parent method. The child method has a different feature, it can identify, if the gender is male or female and assign the proper pronoun(He/She).

However, to learn how to make function and reuse function let us try to develop a program, which calculates the measure of central tendency of a sample (mean, median, mode) and measure of variability (range, variance, standard deviation). In addition to those measures, find the min, max, count, percentile, and frequency distribution of the sample. You can create a class called Statistics and create all the functions that do statistical calculations as methods for the Statistics class. Check the output below.

    OUTPUT 

    ages = [31, 26, 34, 37, 27, 26, 32, 32, 26, 27, 27, 24, 32, 33, 27, 25, 26, 38, 37, 31, 34, 24, 33, 29, 26]

print('Count:', data.count()) # 25

    Challenge

    Exercises: Level 2

    1. Create a class called PersonAccount. It has firstname, lastname, incomes, expenses properties and it has total_income, total_expense, account_info, add_income, add_expense and account_balance methods. Incomes is a set of incomes and its description. The same goes for expenses.

    5.2 File Handling

    File Handling

    So far we have seen different Python data types. We usually store our data in different file formats. In addition to handling files, we will also see different file formats(.txt, .json, .xml, .csv, .tsv, .excel) in this section. First, let us get familiar with handling files with common file format(.txt).

    File handling is an import part of programming which allows us to create, read, update and delete files. In Python to handle data we use open() built-in function.

    PYTHON 

    # Syntax
open('filename', mode) # mode(r, a, w, x, t,b)  could be to read, write, update
    • “r” - Read - Default value. Opens a file for reading, it returns an error if the file does not exist
    • “a” - Append - Opens a file for appending, creates the file if it does not exist
    • “w” - Write - Opens a file for writing, creates the file if it does not exist
    • “x” - Create - Creates the specified file, returns an error if the file exists
    • “t” - Text - Default value. Text mode
    • “b” - Binary - Binary mode (e.g. images)

    Opening Files for Reading

    The default mode of open is reading, so we do not have to specify ‘r’ or ‘rt’. I have created and saved a file named reading_file_example.txt in the files directory. Let us see how it is done:

    PYTHON 

    f = open('./files/reading_file_example.txt')
print(f) # <_io.TextIOWrapper name='./files/reading_file_example.txt' mode='r' encoding='UTF-8'> - the encoding may differ on your computer
f.close()

    As you can see in the example above, I printed the opened file and it gave some information about it. Opened file has different reading methods: read(), readline, readlines. An opened file has to be closed with close() method.

    • read(): read the whole text as string. If we want to limit the number of characters we want to read, we can limit it by passing int value to the read(number) method.

    PYTHON 

    f = open('./files/reading_file_example.txt')
txt = f.read()
print(type(txt))
print(txt)
f.close()

    OUTPUT 

    <class 'str'>
This is an example to show how to open a file and read.
This is the second line of the text.

    Instead of printing all the text, let us print the first 10 characters of the text file.

    PYTHON 

    f = open('./files/reading_file_example.txt')
txt = f.read(10)
print(type(txt))
print(txt)
f.close()

    OUTPUT 

    <class 'str'>
This is an
    • readline(): read only the first line

    PYTHON 

    f = open('./files/reading_file_example.txt')
line = f.readline()
print(type(line))
print(line)
f.close()

    OUTPUT 

    <class 'str'>
This is an example to show how to open a file and read.
    • readlines(): read all the text line by line and returns a list of lines

    PYTHON 

    f = open('./files/reading_file_example.txt')
lines = f.readlines()
print(type(lines))
print(lines)
f.close()

    OUTPUT 

    <class 'list'>
['This is an example to show how to open a file and read.\n', 'This is the second line of the text.']

    Another way to get all the lines as a list is using splitlines():

    PYTHON 

    f = open('./files/reading_file_example.txt')
lines = f.read().splitlines()
print(type(lines))
print(lines)
f.close()

    OUTPUT 

    <class 'list'>
['This is an example to show how to open a file and read.', 'This is the second line of the text.']

    After we open a file, we should close it. There is a high tendency of forgetting to close them. There is a new way of opening files using with - closes the files by itself. Let us rewrite the previous example with the with method:

    PYTHON 

    with open('./files/reading_file_example.txt') as f:
    lines = f.read().splitlines()
    print(type(lines))
    print(lines)

    OUTPUT 

    <class 'list'>
['This is an example to show how to open a file and read.', 'This is the second line of the text.']

    Opening Files for Writing and Updating

    To write to an existing file, we must add a mode as parameter to the open() function:

    • “a” - append - will append to the end of the file, if the file does not exist it creates a new file.
    • “w” - write - will overwrite any existing content, if the file does not exist it creates.

    The code below creates a new file, if the file does not exist:

    PYTHON 

    with open('./files/writing_file_example.txt','w') as f:
    f.write('This text will be written in a newly created file.\n')

    Now let us append some text to the end of that file. Running this again adds the line again, because “a” never removes what is already there:

    PYTHON 

    with open('./files/writing_file_example.txt','a') as f:
    f.write('This text has to be appended at the end.\n')

with open('./files/writing_file_example.txt') as f:
    print(f.read())

    OUTPUT 

    This text will be written in a newly created file.
This text has to be appended at the end.

    Deleting Files

    To remove a file we use the os module. Modules are explained in Week 6, so for now leave the import os line as is.

    PYTHON 

    import os
os.remove('./files/writing_file_example.txt')

    If the file does not exist, the remove method will raise an error, so it is good to use a condition like this:

    PYTHON 

    import os
if os.path.exists('./files/writing_file_example.txt'):
    os.remove('./files/writing_file_example.txt')
else:
    print('The file does not exist')
# The file does not exist - we already removed it above

    File Types

    File with txt Extension

    File with txt extension is a very common form of data and we have covered it in the previous section. Let us move to the JSON file

    File with json Extension

    JSON stands for JavaScript Object Notation. Actually, it is a stringified JavaScript object or Python dictionary.

    Example:

    PYTHON 

    # dictionary
person_dct = {
    "name": "Jack",
    "country": "Australia",
    "city": "Perth",
    "skills": ["Python", "Excel", "SQL"]
}

# JSON: the same data as a string. JSON always uses double quotes
person_json = '{"name": "Jack", "country": "Australia", "city": "Perth", "skills": ["Python", "Excel", "SQL"]}'

# we use three quotes and make it multiple line to make it more readable
person_json = '''{
    "name": "Jack",
    "country": "Australia",
    "city": "Perth",
    "skills": ["Python", "Excel", "SQL"]
}'''

    Changing JSON to Dictionary

    To change a JSON to a dictionary, first we import the json module and then we use loads method.

    PYTHON 

    import json
# JSON
person_json = '''{
    "name": "Jack",
    "country": "Australia",
    "city": "Perth",
    "skills": ["Python", "Excel", "SQL"]
}'''
# let's change JSON to dictionary
person_dct = json.loads(person_json)
print(type(person_dct))
print(person_dct)
print(person_dct['name'])

    OUTPUT 

    <class 'dict'>
{'name': 'Jack', 'country': 'Australia', 'city': 'Perth', 'skills': ['Python', 'Excel', 'SQL']}
Jack

    Changing Dictionary to JSON

    To change a dictionary to a JSON we use dumps method from the json module.

    PYTHON 

    import json
# python dictionary
person = {
    "name": "Jack",
    "country": "Australia",
    "city": "Perth",
    "skills": ["Python", "Excel", "SQL"]
}
# let's convert it to  json
person_json = json.dumps(person, indent=4) # indent could be 2, 4, 8. It beautifies the json
print(type(person_json))
print(person_json)

    When you print it, it does not have the quotes, but it is a string. JSON does not have its own type in Python: it is a string.

    OUTPUT 

    <class 'str'>
{
    "name": "Jack",
    "country": "Australia",
    "city": "Perth",
    "skills": [
        "Python",
        "Excel",
        "SQL"
    ]
}

    Saving as JSON File

    We can also save our data as a json file. Let us save it as a json file using the following steps. For writing a json file, we use the json.dump() method, it can take dictionary, output file, ensure_ascii and indent.

    PYTHON 

    import json
# python dictionary
person = {
    "name": "Jack",
    "country": "Australia",
    "city": "Perth",
    "skills": ["Python", "Excel", "SQL"]
}
with open('./files/json_example.json', 'w', encoding='utf-8') as f:
    json.dump(person, f, ensure_ascii=False, indent=4)

    In the code above, we use encoding and indentation. Indentation makes the json file easy to read.

    File with csv Extension

    CSV stands for comma separated values. CSV is a simple file format used to store tabular data, such as a spreadsheet or database. CSV is a very common data format in data science.

    Example:

    "name","country","city","skills"
"Jack","Australia","Perth","Python"

    Example:

    PYTHON 

    import csv
with open('./files/csv_example.csv') as f:
    csv_reader = csv.reader(f, delimiter=',') # we use, reader method to read csv
    line_count = 0
    for row in csv_reader:
        if line_count == 0:
            print(f'Column names are :{", ".join(row)}')
            line_count += 1
        else:
            print(
                f'\t{row[0]} is a student. He lives in {row[2]}, {row[1]}.')
            line_count += 1
    print(f'Number of lines:  {line_count}')

    OUTPUT 

    Column names are :name, country, city, skills
        Jack is a student. He lives in Perth, Australia.
Number of lines:  2

    File with xlsx Extension

    To read Excel files we need to install the openpyxl package. Installing packages with pip is covered in Week 6, so for now just read this example; it will not run until openpyxl is installed.

    PYTHON 

    import openpyxl
workbook = openpyxl.load_workbook('sample.xlsx')
print(workbook.sheetnames)   # the names of the sheets, e.g. ['Sheet1']

    File with xml Extension

    XML is another structured data format which looks like HTML. In XML the tags are not predefined. The first line is an XML declaration. The person tag is the root of the XML. The person has a gender attribute. Example: XML

    XML 

    <?xml version="1.0"?>
<person gender="male">
  <name>Jack</name>
  <country>Australia</country>
  <city>Perth</city>
  <skills>
    <skill>Python</skill>
    <skill>Excel</skill>
    <skill>SQL</skill>
  </skills>
</person>

    For more information on how to read an XML file check the documentation

    PYTHON 

    import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET
tree = ET.parse('./files/xml_example.xml')
root = tree.getroot()
print('Root tag:', root.tag)
print('Attribute:', root.attrib)
for child in root:
    print('field:', child.tag)

    OUTPUT 

    Root tag: person
Attribute: {'gender': 'male'}
field: name
field: country
field: city
field: skills

    Concepts Bridge: Everything Is an Object, and Floating-Point Risk

    Time: 30 minutes. Part 1: 7 minutes. Part 2: 15 minutes (the 9:16 video plus about 5 minutes of reading and running the code). Activity: 8 minutes.

    Why this matters

    Object-oriented programming in Python starts from one idea: “everything is an object”. Working with numbers safely means knowing about floating-point problems such as the Ariane 5 failure. Both support LO 2 (apply object-oriented techniques) and LO 3 (build to a specification, which includes knowing where your numbers can go wrong).

    Part 1: Everything is an object (about 7 minutes)

    An object is a piece of data bundled with the actions (methods) that work on it. This week you built your own objects with class. Here is the surprise: Python’s built-in values are objects too. Whole numbers, strings, lists and even functions are all objects.

    Two built-in functions let you look inside:

    • type(x) tells you which class an object was made from.
    • id(x) gives a number that identifies that one object while the program runs. Two different objects never share an id at the same time.

    PYTHON 

    print(type(42))
print(type("hello"))
print(type([1, 2, 3]))
print(type(len))

class Dog:
    pass

rex = Dog()
print(type(rex))
print(type(Dog))          # even a class is an object

a = [1, 2, 3]
b = [1, 2, 3]
c = a
print(a == b)             # same contents?
print(a is b)             # same object?
print(a is c)             # c is just another name for a
print(id(a) == id(c))
print((42).bit_length())  # a whole number has methods

    Run it and read the output. A list has methods like .append() because it is an object of the list class. A whole number has methods such as .bit_length() for the same reason.

    Duck typing and dunder methods

    In T#58 you met duck typing: if an object has the method you need, Python does not care what class it is. The saying is “if it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it is a duck”.

    In T#59 you met operator overloading. The link between the two is the dunder method. “Dunder” is short for “double underscore”, such as __init__ or __add__. Python calls these special methods behind the scenes:

    You write Python actually calls
    len(x) x.__len__()
    a + b a.__add__(b)
    str(x) and print(x) x.__str__()
    a == b a.__eq__(b)

    That is why + works on numbers, strings and lists: each class defines its own __add__. It is also why your own class can use len() or + once you define the right dunder method.

    PYTHON 

    print(3 + 4)
print("3" + "4")
print([3] + [4])
print((3).__add__(4))       # exactly what 3 + 4 does

class Basket:
    def __init__(self, items):
        self.items = items

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.items)

    def __add__(self, other):
        return Basket(self.items + other.items)

    def __str__(self):
        return "Basket with " + ", ".join(self.items)

mine = Basket(["apple", "pear"])
yours = Basket(["plum"])
print(len(mine))            # works because of __len__
print(mine + yours)         # works because of __add__ and __str__

    Basket and list are different classes, yet len() works on both. That is duck typing again: len() only asks “do you have __len__?”.

    Optional, if you have time later: Driscoll (2017) Chapter 11, “Classes” (https://web.archive.org/web/20260308142225/https://python101.pythonlibrary.org/chapter11_classes.html). It is not part of the 30 minutes.

    Part 2: Floating-point risk (about 15 minutes)

    Watch first (9:16, about 10 minutes with pauses)

    [Computerphile] Floating Point Numbers (9:16) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PZRI1IfStY0

    Look for how a computer stores a number using a fixed number of binary digits, and why some decimal numbers cannot be stored exactly.

    Why 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3

    Computers store numbers in binary (base 2). In the decimal system you cannot write one third exactly (0.3333…). In binary, you cannot write one tenth exactly. Python’s float type stores the closest value it can fit, so tiny errors creep in.

    PYTHON 

    print(0.1 + 0.2)
print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)
print(f"{0.1:.20f}")       # see the real stored value of 0.1
print(round(0.1 + 0.2, 2) == 0.3)

    The first line prints 0.30000000000000004. The comparison is False. This is not a Python bug. Almost every language that uses standard floating-point numbers behaves this way.

    Two safe habits:

    1. Never compare floats with ==. Compare with a tolerance, such as math.isclose(a, b).
    2. For money, use whole cents (integers) or the Decimal type.

    PYTHON 

    import math
print(math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3))

    The Decimal type

    decimal.Decimal stores numbers as decimal digits, so 0.1 really is 0.1. It is slower than float, but exact for the sums people do by hand. Always create a Decimal from a string. If you pass a float, the float’s error comes along too.

    PYTHON 

    from decimal import Decimal

print(Decimal("0.1") + Decimal("0.2"))
print(Decimal("0.1") + Decimal("0.2") == Decimal("0.3"))
print(Decimal(0.1))        # the float's error is copied in
print(Decimal("19.95") * 3)

    Case study: Ariane 5 (1996)

    On 4 June 1996 the first Ariane 5 rocket broke up about 37 seconds after launch. Software reused from Ariane 4 tried to convert a 64-bit floating-point value into a 16-bit signed whole number. The faster Ariane 5 produced a value too big to fit, the overflow stopped the inertial reference system computers (both the primary and the backup), and the rocket lost its guidance data. Number types have limits, so check that a value fits before you convert it (Lions, 1996).

    Activity (about 8 minutes)

    1. Without running it, predict the output of each line:

      PYTHON 

      print(0.1 * 3)
print(0.1 * 3 == 0.3)
print(type(0.1 * 3))
print(type(Decimal("0.1") * 3))

      Then run it (add from decimal import Decimal at the top) and check your predictions.

    2. A shop sells an item for 0.10 dollars. Add up the price 10 times in a loop using a float, then using a Decimal. Compare each total with 1. What do you notice?

    3. In two sentences, explain to a classmate why len("abc") and len([1, 2]) both work. Use the words “object” and “dunder method”.

    Model answer

    1. Predictions: 0.30000000000000004, False, <class 'float'>, <class 'decimal.Decimal'>.
    2. The float total is 0.9999999999999999, so total == 1 is False. The Decimal total is exactly 1.0, so the comparison is True.
    3. Strings and lists are both objects, and each of their classes defines a __len__ dunder method. len() simply calls __len__ on whatever object it is given, which is duck typing.

    Working code for questions 1 and 2:

    PYTHON 

    from decimal import Decimal

print(0.1 * 3)
print(0.1 * 3 == 0.3)
print(type(0.1 * 3))
print(type(Decimal("0.1") * 3))

float_total = 0.0
decimal_total = Decimal("0")
for _ in range(10):
    float_total += 0.1
    decimal_total += Decimal("0.1")

print(float_total, float_total == 1)
print(decimal_total, decimal_total == 1)

    Reference

    • Lions, J.L. (1996) Ariane 5 Flight 501 Failure: Report by the Inquiry Board. Paris: European Space Agency.

    Practice task: Animal Class and Mini Project (Part 1)

    Callout

    Files for this task

    Download these files into a folder for this task and open the folder in PyCharm.

    • animal_starter.py
    • animal_solution.py
    • test_animal.py
    • library_starter.py
    • library.py
    • test_library.py

    Build block: 2 hours. This is practice, not an assessment. There are no marks. Use the tests to check yourself.

    Part Task Time
    1 Animal class (steps 1 to 4 and 6; step 5 is an optional stretch) about 30 minutes
    2 Mini project, Part 1: library loan manager about 90 minutes
    Total 2 hours

    The mini project is the bigger task, so it gets most of the time. If the Animal class runs over, skip step 5 and move on.

    You will need Section 5.1 (classes), Section 5.2 (files and JSON) and Section 4.4 (try/except, from Week 4).

    Part 1: Animal class (about 30 minutes, plus about 15 for the optional step 5)

    Goal

    Write a class, make several objects from it, then write a subclass (a class that inherits from another). This is a classic first OOP exercise: one class, many objects.

    Key terms:

    • Class: a blueprint for objects.
    • Object (or instance): one thing built from the blueprint. Animal("Mittens", ...) and Animal("Daisy", ...) are two instances.
    • Attribute: a variable that belongs to an object, such as self.name.
    • Subclass: a class that inherits the attributes and methods of a parent class and can add or replace some.

    Steps

    Open animal_starter.py and work through TODO 1 to 6. Step 5 is an optional stretch.

    1. Animal takes name, species, sound and age (age defaults to 0). Store all four on self.

    2. speak() returns (does not print) text such as "Mittens says Meow".

    3. have_birthday() adds 1 to the animal’s age.

    4. __str__() returns text such as "Mittens the cat (age 3)". Python uses it when you print() the object.

    5. Optional stretch: Dog inherits from Animal. Its __init__ takes only name and age=0 and calls super().__init__(...) with species "dog" and sound "Woof". It overrides speak() (replaces the parent’s version) to return "Rex says Woof! Woof!", and adds a new method fetch(item) returning "Rex fetches the ball".

    6. In the if __name__ == "__main__": block, create at least two Animal objects. Print each, call speak(), give one a birthday, and print it again. If you did step 5, add a Dog too and call fetch().

      Leave the line if __name__ == "__main__": exactly as it is in the starter and put your test code inside that block. Week 6 explains why it is there; for now, just treat it as “run this part when I press Run”.

    Example output 

    Mittens the cat (age 3)
Mittens says Meow
Daisy the cow (age 0)
Daisy says Moo
Rex the dog (age 2)
Rex says Woof! Woof!
Rex the dog (age 3)
Rex fetches the ball

    Hints

    • Inside a method, self means “this object”. Every method’s first parameter is self.
    • Use return in speak(), not print(). Returned text is easier to test.
    • Changing one object’s age must not change another’s. If it does, check that you used self.age.
    • Stuck on super()? Compare with the Student(Person) example in Section 5.1 (Inheritance).

    Check your work

    Tests for Dog are skipped until you write it. Further stretch (optional): add a Cat subclass whose speak() is different, then loop over a list holding an Animal, a Dog and a Cat and call speak() on each. That is polymorphism and duck typing (T#57 and T#58) in action.

    Part 2: Mini project, Part 1 (about 90 minutes)

    Go to mini_project/README.md. You will build a library loan manager with a Book class, a Library class and JSON saving. Week 6 finishes it.

    Running the tests

    Tests are small programs that check your code. We use pytest.

    1. Open test_animal.py. Near the top, change MODULE_NAME = "animal_solution" to MODULE_NAME = "animal_starter". Now the tests check your code.

    2. In PyCharm, right-click test_animal.py and choose Run ‘pytest in test_animal.py’. Or, in the Terminal tab, from the repository root:

      python -m pytest weeks/week-5/practice/test_animal.py

    3. Read any failure message from the top. It names the test and shows what it expected.

    Peek at animal_solution.py only after you have tried each step yourself. The same method works for the mini project with test_library.py.

    If pytest is missing, run python -m pip install pytest in the Terminal tab.

    Mini Project, Part 1: Library Loan Manager

    Time: about 90 minutes. This is practice, not an assessment. There are no marks.

    What you are building

    A small library system. It keeps track of books, lets you lend and return them, and saves everything to a JSON file so nothing is lost when the program stops.

    You will use ideas from this week: classes (Section 5.1), a dictionary of objects, try/except (Week 4), and saving to JSON (Section 5.2).

    Files

    File What it is
    library_starter.py Your work. It has TODOs to fill in.
    test_library.py Tests that check your work.
    library.py The model solution. Look only after you have tried.

    Steps

    Open library_starter.py and work through the TODOs in order.

    1. The Book class (about 30 minutes)

    • __init__(self, title, author, isbn) stores the three values. It also sets self.on_loan = False.

    • to_dict(self) returns a dictionary: {"title": ..., "author": ..., "isbn": ..., "on_loan": ...}.

    • __str__(self) returns text like:

      Dune by Frank Herbert (111) - available
Dune by Frank Herbert (111) - on loan

    • from_dict is already written for you. It uses @classmethod. A class method belongs to the class instead of one object, and its first parameter is cls (the class itself). That lets Book.from_dict(data) build a new Book from a dictionary, which is how a book comes back from the saved file. Read it, but you do not need to change it.

    2. The Library class (about 35 minutes)
    • __init__ creates self.books = {}. The key is each book’s isbn and the value is the Book object. (An ISBN is a book’s unique number. We use short text codes like "111".)
    • add_book(book) stores the book under its isbn.
    • lend(isbn) sets on_loan to True.
      • Unknown isbn: Python raises KeyError for you if you write self.books[isbn].
      • Book already on loan: raise ValueError("...") with a helpful message (see the raise hint below).
    • return_book(isbn) sets on_loan to False.
      • Unknown isbn: KeyError.
      • Book not on loan: ValueError.
    • available_books() returns a list of the Book objects that are not on loan.
    3. Saving and loading (about 15 minutes, then 10 to run it and check)
    • save(path) is already written for you. Read it: it turns each book into a dictionary with to_dict(), puts them in a list, and uses json.dump(data, file, indent=2).
    • load(path) is yours to write. It reads the file, turns each dictionary back into a Book with Book.from_dict(...), and replaces self.books. Wrap the file reading in try/except FileNotFoundError. If the file does not exist yet, leave the library empty and do not crash.

    Try it yourself

    After the tests pass, add a short block at the bottom of library_starter.py:

    PYTHON 

    if __name__ == "__main__":
    library = Library()
    library.add_book(Book("Dune", "Frank Herbert", "111"))
    library.add_book(Book("Emma", "Jane Austen", "222"))
    library.lend("111")
    for book in library.books.values():
        print(book)
    library.save("library.json")

    Leave the line if __name__ == "__main__": as it is and put your test code inside that block. Week 6 explains why it is there.

    Open library.json and look at the saved text.

    Hints

    • raise means “stop here and signal an error on purpose”. You choose the error type and the message:

      PYTHON 

      if book.on_loan:
    raise ValueError("Dune is already on loan")

      Python stops the method at that line, and the error message appears unless some other code catches it with try/except. The tests check that the right error is raised.

    • Use the keys "title", "author", "isbn" and "on_loan" exactly. Other code (and Week 6) depends on these names.

    • Write the to_dict and __str__ code first and test it, then move on.

    • "on loan" if book.on_loan else "available" is a handy one-line way to choose between two words.

    • with open(path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as file: closes the file for you.

    • In PyCharm, the tmp_path in the tests is a temporary folder that pytest creates and cleans up. Your real files are never touched.

    Running the tests

    1. Open test_library.py. Change MODULE_NAME = "library" to MODULE_NAME = "library_starter" so the tests check your code.

    2. Right-click the file in PyCharm and choose Run ‘pytest in test_library.py’, or run this in the Terminal from the repository root:

      python -m pytest weeks/week-5/practice/mini_project

    Check your work

    Coming in Week 6 (Part 2)

    In Week 6 you will finish this project. You will move the classes into a proper module (a reusable .py file) and write a separate program file with a text menu so a person can add, lend and return books without writing code. You will add a search feature (for example, finding books by title or author) and add type hints (notes that say what type each value should be) so your code is easier to read and check. Keep the names in this Part 1 exactly as they are: Week 6 builds on them.

    Key Points
    • Each week has four blocks: Watch, Read & practise, Concepts Bridge and Build.
    • A class is a blueprint; an object is one thing made from it.
    • self refers to the current object.
    • A child class inherits from its parent and can override its methods.
    • Use with open(…) so the file closes itself.
    • Mode “w” overwrites, “a” appends, “r” reads.
    • json.dump() and json.load() save and load Python data.
    • Every value in Python is an object with a type and methods.
    • Floats are approximations; use Decimal when exact values matter.
    • Classes keep data and behaviour together.
    • JSON files let a program remember data between runs.

    Content from Week 6: Modules, libraries and choosing a paradigm

    Last updated on 2026-11-03 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 319 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • What will I learn in Week 6, and how should I spend my 6 hours?
    • How do I split code into files and use code others have written?
    • How do I install and use third-party packages?
    • How do I use packages safely?
    • How do I choose a paradigm for a problem?
    • Can I finish a complete program and justify its design?

    Objectives

    • Plan your study time for the week using the time plan.
    • Create and import your own module.
    • Use built-in modules such as math, random, os and statistics.
    • Install, list and remove packages with pip.
    • Fetch data from the web with requests.
    • Create a simple package of your own.
    • Add type hints to a function.
    • Describe the risks of third-party libraries.
    • Compare paradigms using a set of criteria.
    • Finish the library-loan manager across modules, and compare two paradigms in it.

    Week 6 overview

    Theme: split your code into modules, use other people’s code safely, and decide which programming style suits a problem.

    This is the last week. You also finish the mini project you started in Week 5.

    Learning goals

    By the end of this week you can:

    1. Write your own module and import it, and explain what if __name__ == "__main__": does.
    2. Use built-in modules such as random and math.
    3. Install a third-party package with pip inside a virtual environment, and say why pinning versions matters.
    4. Explain, in a few sentences, which programming paradigm (style) suits a problem and why.

    Concepts Bridge 30 min bridge.md: type safety, library risk, choosing a paradigm

    Section 6.1: Modules (about 22 min)

    6.1 Modules

    Modules

    What is a Module

    A module is a file containing a set of codes or a set of functions which can be included to an application. A module could be a file containing a single variable, a function or a big code base.

    Creating a Module

    To create a module we write our codes in a python script and we save it as a .py file. Create a file named mymodule.py inside your project folder. Let us write some code in this file.

    PYTHON 

    # mymodule.py file
def generate_full_name(firstname, lastname):
    space = ' '
    fullname = firstname + space + lastname
    return fullname


def sum_two_nums(num1, num2):
    return num1 + num2


gravity = 9.81
person = {
    "firstname": "Jack",
    "age": 25,
    "country": "Australia",
    "city": "Perth"
}

    Create main.py file in your project directory and import the mymodule.py file.

    Importing a Module

    To import the file we use the import keyword and the name of the file only.

    PYTHON 

    # main.py file
import mymodule
print(mymodule.generate_full_name('Jack', 'Wilson')) # Jack Wilson

    Import Functions from a Module

    We can have many functions in a file and we can import all the functions differently.

    PYTHON 

    # main.py file
from mymodule import generate_full_name, sum_two_nums, person, gravity
print(generate_full_name('Jack','Wilson'))  # Jack Wilson
print(sum_two_nums(1,9))                     # 10
mass = 100
weight = mass * gravity
print(weight)                                # 981.0
print(person['firstname'])                   # Jack

    Import Functions from a Module and Renaming

    During importing we can rename the name of the module.

    PYTHON 

    # main.py file
from mymodule import generate_full_name as fullname, sum_two_nums as total, person as p, gravity as g
print(fullname('Jack','Wilson'))  # Jack Wilson
print(total(1, 9))                # 10
mass = 100
weight = mass * g
print(weight)                     # 981.0
print(p)                          # {'firstname': 'Jack', 'age': 25, 'country': 'Australia', 'city': 'Perth'}
print(p['firstname'])             # Jack

    Import Built-in Modules

    Like other programming languages we can also import modules by importing the file/function using the key word import. Let’s import the common module we will use most of the time. Some of the common built-in modules: math, datetime, os,sys, random, statistics, collections, json,re

    OS Module

    Using python os module it is possible to automatically perform many operating system tasks. The OS module in Python provides functions for creating, changing current working directory, and removing a directory (folder), fetching its contents, changing and identifying the current directory.

    PYTHON 

    # import the module
import os
# Getting the current working directory (the folder Python is working in)
print(os.getcwd())                         # e.g. C:\Users\jack\IntroToProgramming
# Creating a directory
os.mkdir('practice_folder')
print(os.path.exists('practice_folder'))   # True
# Removing a directory (it must be empty)
os.rmdir('practice_folder')
print(os.path.exists('practice_folder'))   # False
# os.chdir('some_folder') changes the current directory to some_folder

    Sys Module

    The sys module provides functions and variables used to manipulate different parts of the Python runtime environment. Function sys.argv returns a list of command line arguments passed to a Python script. The item at index 0 in this list is always the name of the script, at index 1 is the argument passed from the command line.

    Example of a script.py file:

    PYTHON 

    import sys
# print(sys.argv[0], sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2])  # this line would print out: filename argument1 argument2
print('Welcome {}. Enjoy {}!'.format(sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]))

    To check how this script works, run this in the terminal (the quotes keep “Intro to Programming” as one argument):

    BASH 

    python script.py Jack "Intro to Programming"

    The result:

    BASH 

    Welcome Jack. Enjoy Intro to Programming!

    Some useful sys commands:

    PYTHON 

    import sys
# To know the largest integer variable it takes
print(sys.maxsize)   # 9223372036854775807 on a 64-bit computer
# To know the folders Python searches for modules
print(sys.path)
# To know the version of python you are using
print(sys.version)   # e.g. 3.12.10 (...)
# To stop the program straight away
sys.exit()

    Statistics Module

    The statistics module provides functions for mathematical statistics of numeric data. The popular statistical functions which are defined in this module: mean, median, mode, stdev etc.

    PYTHON 

    from statistics import * # importing all the statistics modules
ages = [20, 20, 24, 24, 25, 22, 26, 20, 23, 22, 26]
print(mean(ages))       # ~22.9
print(median(ages))     # 23
print(mode(ages))       # 20
print(stdev(ages))      # ~2.3

    Math Module

    Module containing many mathematical operations and constants.

    PYTHON 

    import math
print(math.pi)           # 3.141592653589793, pi constant
print(math.sqrt(2))      # 1.4142135623730951, square root
print(math.pow(2, 3))    # 8.0, exponential function
print(math.floor(9.81))  # 9, rounding to the lowest
print(math.ceil(9.81))   # 10, rounding to the highest
print(math.log10(100))   # 2.0, logarithm with 10 as base

    Now, we have imported the math module which contains lots of function which can help us to perform mathematical calculations. To check what functions the module has got, we can use help(math), or dir(math). This will display the available functions in the module. If we want to import only a specific function from the module we import it as follows:

    PYTHON 

    from math import pi
print(pi)  # 3.141592653589793

    It is also possible to import multiple functions at once

    PYTHON 

    from math import pi, sqrt, pow, floor, ceil, log10
print(pi)                 # 3.141592653589793
print(sqrt(2))            # 1.4142135623730951
print(pow(2, 3))          # 8.0
print(floor(9.81))        # 9
print(ceil(9.81))         # 10
print(log10(100))         # 2.0

    But if we want to import all the function in math module we can use * .

    PYTHON 

    from math import *
print(pi)                  # 3.141592653589793, pi constant
print(sqrt(2))             # 1.4142135623730951, square root
print(pow(2, 3))           # 8.0, exponential
print(floor(9.81))         # 9, rounding to the lowest
print(ceil(9.81))          # 10, rounding to the highest
print(log10(100))          # 2.0

    When we import we can also rename the name of the function.

    PYTHON 

    from math import pi as  PI
print(PI) # 3.141592653589793

    String Module

    A string module is a useful module for many purposes. The example below shows some use of the string module.

    PYTHON 

    import string
print(string.ascii_letters) # abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ
print(string.digits)        # 0123456789
print(string.punctuation)   # !"#$%&'()*+,-./:;<=>?@[\]^_`{|}~

    Random Module

    By now you are familiar with importing modules. Let us do one more import to get very familiar with it. Let us import random module which gives us a random number between 0 and 0.9999…. The random module has lots of functions but in this section we will only use random and randint.

    PYTHON 

    from random import random, randint
print(random())   # it doesn't take any arguments; it returns a value between 0 and 0.9999, e.g. 0.6394
print(randint(5, 20)) # it returns a random integer between 5 and 20 inclusive, e.g. 13
    Challenge

    Exercises: Level 1

    1. Write a function which generates a six digit/character random_user_id.

      OUTPUT 

        print(random_user_id())
  '1ee33d'

    2. Modify the previous task. Declare a function named user_id_gen_by_user. It doesn’t take any parameters but it takes two inputs using input(). One of the inputs is the number of characters and the second input is the number of IDs which are supposed to be generated.

    OUTPUT 

    print(user_id_gen_by_user()) # user input: 5 5
#output:
#kcsy2
#SMFYb
#bWmeq
#ZXOYh
#2Rgxf

print(user_id_gen_by_user()) # 16 5
#1GCSgPLMaBAVQZ26
#YD7eFwNQKNs7qXaT
#ycArC5yrRupyG00S
#UbGxOFI7UXSWAyKN
#dIV0SSUTgAdKwStr
    1. Write a function named rgb_color_gen. It will generate rgb colors (3 values ranging from 0 to 255 each).

    OUTPUT

# rgb(125,244,255) - the output should be in this form

    2. Write a function list_of_rgb_colors which returns any number of RGB colors in an array.
    3. Write a function generate_colors which can generate any number of hexa or rgb colors.

    OUTPUT

   generate_colors('hexa', 1) # ['#b334ef']
